newsitem.title: UK: Steel slowdown hits nickel, but 1997 seen brighter.
newsitem.headline: Steel slowdown hits nickel, but 1997 seen brighter.

text.p: After two years of explosive growth, world stainless steel producers found in 1996 that they had to cut production as customers drew on stocks, economic growth in Europe and Asia slowed and prices fell.
At the same time nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) have fallen steadily since February after a sharp, but brief rally in January.
On Monday benchmark three month nickel futures dropped to a fresh 2-1/4 year low of around $6,410 a tonne from $6,476 on Friday and a high this year of $8,850 hit in February.
Metal traders and analysts said depressed LME nickel prices should come as no surprise given that stainless steel accounts for two thirds of Western world nickel consumption.
But the outlook for 1997 is more bullish, with analysts broadly favouring a resumption of growth in stainless steel output, and with it a rise in primary nickel demand.
"The general economic outlook for 1997 seems to be pretty good," said Ivor Kirman, Marketing Director of Inco Europe Ltd, part of Canadian nickel giant Inco Ltd.
"And if you've got generally favourable world economic conditions for 1997 then that will be reflected in stronger consumption of nickel-containing products," he added.
The most important of these is stainless steel. Some analysts are looking for growth in output of over five percent next year.

In the latest commodity review from the Flemings Global Mining Group world stainless steel production is forecast to increase 5.5 percent to 15.40 million tonnes after dropping nearly two percent to 14.60 million in 1995.
In 1994 and 1995 the world steel market grew by 12 and 13 percent respectively, Flemings estimated.
The impact of lower steel output on primary nickel demand this year was exaggerated by big supplies of cheap stainless scrap, which mills used as an alternative to nickel.
This, added to rising stocks of nickel on the LME, may delay any impact rising stainless output has on primary nickel demand.
LME stocks have risen steadily this year, reflecting sluggish demand. On Monday they stood at 49,548 tonnes, the highest level since November 1995 and well above the 1996 low of 32,010 tonnes.
But the de-stocking phase, both of primary nickel and stainless steel scrap, should not be long, analysts said.

"Once excess stocks of nickel and stainless steel scrap are worked off (by the first quarter of 1997) we believe that nickel prices could rally strongly in 1997," said Macquarie Equities in a recent commodities report.

Macquarie forecasts a five percent rise in nickel demand in 1997, while Flemings expects it to grow over six percent. This should push the supply/demand balance into a small deficit after being roughly balanced in 1996.
While the outlook for nickel prices looks bullish, stainless steel values may struggle to keep pace because stainless output capacity is pegged to grow faster than actual production.
"The rise in stainless steel prices currently underway is likely to be muted because the production rise next year is less than half the capacity rise," Macquarie said.
